THIS CHAPTER IN 60 SECONDS
  • Fiscal anchor: from FY2026-27 the anchor changes from fiscal deficit to debt-to-GDP; target 50 ± 1% by FY31. Fiscal deficit stays the day-to-day tool.
  • GST 2.0 (Sept 2025): two main rates, 5% merit and 18% standard, plus 40% de-merit for sin goods. It is one leg of the "Tripod of Reforms" with the 2019 corporate tax cut and the April 2025 income-tax reform.
  • 16th Finance Commission: states' share stays 41%; formula adds a GDP-contribution criterion; centre to reach 3.5% fiscal deficit by FY31; states capped at 3% of GSDP.
  • MSMEs (new limits from Budget 2025), microfinance, IBC, the corporate bond market, cost of capital and the PLI scheme are the finance-and-industry strand of the chapter.
  • Gender budgeting: three parts (A 100%, B 30-99%, C below 30% allocation for women).
Understand it firstThink of the economy as a house. The government's fiscal rules are the wiring limits (how much it may borrow). GST and the Finance Commission decide how the rent is collected and shared between the centre and the states. MSMEs, banks, bonds and PLI are the rooms where money is actually used. The cost of capital is the electricity bill every room pays. This picture is a memory aid, not from the handout.
WORDS YOU NEED FIRST
WordPlain meaning (aid: verify before quoting)
Fiscal anchorThe one target that limits government borrowing in the long run. The handout defines it as a target that limits fiscal policy to ensure long-term debt sustainability.
Glide pathThe year-by-year route down to a target.
DevolutionThe share of central taxes that goes to states.
Off-budget borrowingBorrowing done by a public agency for the government but not counted in the official deficit.
RecourseThe right to claim the money back from the seller if the buyer does not pay. "Without recourse" means the financier cannot.
CIRPCorporate Insolvency Resolution Process under the IBC.
HaircutThe part of a loan that lenders give up in a resolution.
Cost of capitalThe interest rate and return a firm must pay to get money for investment.
Incremental salesExtra sales above a base year; PLI pays only on these.
RememberOne line to carry: The handout links who borrows (fiscal anchor, 16th FC) to who lends (banks, bonds, MFIs, IBC) to who produces (MSMEs, PLI); the cost of capital ties all three.

1 · FISCAL ANCHORING IN INDIA: FROM FLEXIBILITY TO RESPONSIBILITY
PYQ 2013 · 10m · FRBM Act 2003: reasons, salient features, effectiveness (your file)Handout p.51
Understand it firstA fiscal anchor is the ship's anchor of the budget: however the wind blows (wars, slowdowns), the government promises not to drift beyond a fixed limit. The old anchor was the annual fiscal deficit (a one-year snapshot). The new anchor is total debt as a share of GDP (the whole accumulated borrowing). Memory aid, not from the handout.
  • Budget 2025 shifted the fiscal anchor from the fiscal-deficit-to-GDP ratio to the debt-to-GDP ratio, starting FY 2026-27.
  • Fiscal anchor = a target that limits the government's fiscal policy so that long-term debt stays sustainable and macroeconomic stability is kept.
  • "Debt-GDP is a more reliable measure of fiscal performance" - Government's Fiscal Statement 2024.
  • New framework: central government debt-to-GDP of 50 ± 1% by FY31.
  • Fiscal deficit remains the operational tool; debt sustainability becomes the primary anchor.
  • Rationale: greater policy flexibility in a volatile geopolitical and geoeconomic environment.
  • The debt-to-GDP ratio for FY27-FY31 is projected under three nominal GDP growth scenarios: 10%, 10.5% and 11%.
Reasons for the policy shift
Why debt-to-GDP
Better reflection of responsibility: deficit is an annual snapshot; debt-GDP shows cumulative borrowing over time (holistic view)
Medium-term planning and flexibility: a realistic glide path; counter-cyclical spending in downturns, consolidation in growth phases
Supports productive public investment: space for capital expenditure
Fiscal transparency and accountability
Global convergence: advanced economies and the IMF now prefer debt-based metrics
Long-term prudence with growth sensitivity
Challenges in shifting to the debt-GDP ratio
  • FRBM mandates (40% debt-GDP and 3% FD): the current debt level (~57%) is far off, so reducing it takes several years, delaying fiscal consolidation.
  • Off-budget and contingent liabilities understate actual debt: borrowings through PSUs, FCI and NSSF are not always reflected in official debt.
  • No independent Fiscal Council yet (N.K. Singh Committee recommendation): hampers independent scrutiny and accountability of fiscal targets.
  • Crowding out of the private sector: high government borrowing (Centre + States) consumes a large part of domestic savings.
Way forward
  • Calibrated shift to the debt-GDP anchor (N.K. Singh Committee).
  • Promote cooperative fiscal federalism.
  • Strengthen the disinvestment strategy.
  • Promote outcome-based budgeting.

2 · GOODS AND SERVICES TAX REFORMS
PYQ 2019 · 10m · GST: indirect taxes subsumed, revenue implicationsPYQ 2020 · 15m · GST (Compensation to States) Act 2017 and COVID federal tensionHandout pp.52-53 (teacher's handwriting)
Understand it firstGST replaced a maze of central and state indirect taxes with one tax. GST 2.0 (September 2025) is the clean-up: fewer rates, cheaper essentials, and a heavy rate on sin goods. The teacher's page ties it to the revenue story: collections hit all-time highs while growth tracks nominal GDP. Memory aid, not from the handout.
Prevailing scenario
  • Lower inflation: GST revenue growth has broadly aligned with prevailing nominal GDP growth (teacher's chart: gross GST collections reach all-time highs, even as growth tracks nominal GDP).
  • Steady expansion of tax base, observed using High Frequency Indicators (HFI) such as the E-way bill.
  • Two-rate structure with a standard rate of 18%, a merit rate of 5% and a special de-merit (sin-good) rate of 40% for a select few goods and services.
High Frequency Indicators (teacher's box)Meaning
Higher E-way bill generationmore goods movement
Improved Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI)business activity expanding
Record festive season automobile salesstrong demand
Robust UPI transactionsdigital spending
Increased tractor salesrural demand
MNEMONICPUFETPMI · UPI · Festive auto sales · E-way bills · Tractor sales: the five High Frequency Indicators in the teacher's red box. Say it: "GST tax base is PUFET-ing (puffing) up." (own memory aid)
Changes introduced: rate rationalisation
  • Part of the "Tripod of Reforms" undertaken to lower tax incidence and improve price competitiveness.
Tripod of Reforms
Corporate tax reductions of 2019
Personal income tax reforms, April 2025
GST 2.0 reforms of Sept 2025
Key changes introduced in GST 2.0 (handout table)
SectorChange
Agriculture and fertilisersGST on agricultural machinery reduced 12% → 5%; key fertiliser inputs (sulphuric acid, nitric acid, ammonia) 18% → 5%.
AutomobileVehicle category and engine-size based reductions.
Electronic appliancesACs, large TVs, dishwashing machines, monitors and projectors 28% → 18%.
Textiles and labour-intensive goodsMan-made fibres 18% → 5%; man-made yarn 12% → 5%; handicrafts, marble and intermediate leather goods 12% → 5%.
Everyday essentials and foodHousehold items shifted to 5%. UHT milk, Indian breads and pre-packaged labelled paneer made zero GST.
Medicines and medical equipmentSelect life-saving drugs zero GST; other drugs and medicines 12% → 5%; medical apparatus, devices and equipment at 5%.
Hotel and personal servicesHotel rooms up to ₹7,500/day 12% → 5%; gyms, salons, barbers, yoga centres 18% → 5%.
Insurance policiesGST exemption for individual life and health insurance policies and their reinsurance.

Impacts of GST 2.0 reforms (teacher)
Reduction in tax burden
Lower cost of living
Improve affordability
Stimulate household consumption demand
  • Simplified two-rate structure: reduces transaction costs, eases compliance, helps formalisation of small businesses.
  • Correcting the inverted duty structure, e.g. in key labour-intensive and agri-input sectors such as textiles and fertilisers.
Suggestions for further reforms (teacher)
  • E-way bill system: move from enforcement control to facilitator of smooth logistics (teacher strikes out "enforcement control" and ticks "facilitator of smooth logistics").
  • "Trusted dealer" framework.
  • Wider use of e-seals and electronic locking systems.
  • State governments: shift towards risk-based, system-generated alerts and limit discretionary checks.
GST 1.0 (2017) versus GST 2.0 (2025)
DimensionGST 1.0 (2017)GST 2.0 (2025)
Rate structure4 main slabs: 5%, 12%, 18%, 28% + cess on luxury / sin goodsSimplified to 5% (merit), 18% (standard); 40% de-merit rate for sin / luxury goods
CoverageBroad base, but many exemptions like alcohol, petroleum, outside GSTStill excludes alcohol and petroleum, but expanded coverage of services like the digital economy focus
Consumer goods impactMany essentials (toothpaste, soaps, medicines) taxed at 12% or 18%Essentials, medicines and agri-machinery shifted to 5% or nil, relief for the common man
Compensation to states14% guaranteed growth compensation for 5 years (till 2022), funded by cessNo compensation scheme; instead assurance of timely transfers along with revenue adjustments
Equity concernsHigher slabs on essentials seen as regressiveAims at progressivity: lower rates on essentials, higher rates on luxury / sin goods
Ease of doing businessBlocked working capital, refund delaysSimplified ITC rules, quicker refunds, reduced classification disputes

3 · NON-TAX REVENUE AND EQUITY MONETISATION
Handout p.53 (teacher's handwriting)
  • Stable: non-tax revenue about 1.4% of GDP in post-pandemic times.
  • Non-tax revenues strengthened through: higher surplus transfers from the RBI; improved financial performance of public sector banks and financial institutions.
  • Disinvestment: in about 30% of CPSEs, government shareholding is below 60%, so there is limited space for disinvestment.
  • Equity monetisation pipeline stabilised by revising the definition of "Government Company": presently the government must hold at least 51%; proposed minimum 26% ownership, leaving room to monetise stake while retaining special resolution rights.
  • Disinvestment receipts could be earmarked for strategic investments in emerging tech and innovation-driven companies.
Check thisp.53: the teacher's note says "In about 30% of CPSE, govt. shareholding < 60%" and the pink box gives 51% → 26%. The handwriting is clear; the "Government Company" definition change is a proposal in the teacher's words ("proposed to have"), so write "proposed" in answers.
Short forms in section 3

CPSE = Central Public Sector Enterprise (a company owned by the central government)

GDP = Gross Domestic Product (value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a year)

RBI = Reserve Bank of India (India's central bank)

4 · 16TH FINANCE COMMISSION RECOMMENDATIONS
PYQ 2025 · 15m · Fiscal Health Index of states (your file)Handout p.54
Understand it firstThe Finance Commission is the referee between the Centre and the states. The 16th FC keeps the states' slice at 41% but changes how it is cut (it adds a GDP-contribution test and drops the tax-effort test) and ties grants and borrowing to discipline (3% of GSDP, no off-budget loans). Memory aid, not from the handout.
ItemRecommendation (handout)
Tax devolutionStates' share in central taxes remains 41%.
Devolution formulaRevised using income distance, population, demographic performance, area, forest cover and a new GDP contribution criterion.
Grants-in-aidTotal grants of ₹9.47 lakh crore for local bodies and disaster management.
Revenue deficit grantsRevenue-deficit, sector-specific and state-specific grants discontinued.
Local body grants₹7.91 lakh crore for rural and urban local bodies.
Performance-linked grantsLinked to audited accounts, State Finance Commission and own-revenue growth.
Disaster management grantsCentre's share of ₹1.56 lakh crore.
Centre fiscal deficit roadmapReduce fiscal deficit to 3.5% of GDP by FY31.
State fiscal deficit limitCapped at 3% of GSDP. States to pursue DISCOM privatisation for power-sector reform.
Off-budget borrowingsTo be strictly discontinued and included in deficit / debt calculation.
Debt roadmapCombined Centre-State debt to fall from 77.3% to 73.1% of GDP.
Subsidy rationalisationReview untargeted subsidies and unconditional cash transfers; standard accounting of subsidies and transfers across states.
State PSE reformsReview and closure of 308 inactive State Public Sector Enterprises.
Key concerns about the 16th FC
Concerns
States' tax share retained at 41% despite rising expenditure responsibilities
Cesses and surcharges excluded from the divisible pool, reducing effective transfers
Revenue deficit grants discontinued: hurts fiscally weaker states
Sector-specific and state-specific grants discontinued: reduces targeted support
GDP contribution criterion added: may favour economically larger states
Tax and fiscal effort criterion removed: weakens incentive for own-revenue mobilisation
Performance-linked local body grants: difficult for weaker bodies with poor accounts
Strict 3% GSDP deficit limit: may reduce fiscal flexibility
Ban on off-budget borrowings: improves transparency but limits flexibility
Subsidy rationalisation: politically difficult, may affect welfare delivery
DISCOM privatisation push: political and labour resistance
State PSE closure / disinvestment: employment and regional development concerns

5 · GENDER BUDGETING
PYQ 2016 · 12.5m · gender budgeting: requirements and status (your file)Handout p.55 (teacher's handwriting)
  • Definition: gender budgeting is a strategy that uses fiscal policy and administration to promote gender equality and development of women and girls.
  • Started in 2005-06 as a fiscal innovation. Every year a Gender Budget Statement is published along with the annual Budget.
YearMilestone (journey infographic, MWCD)
2005-06Gender Budgeting adopted by Gol; Statement 13 reports allocations for women and girls
2007Ministry of Finance issued a Charter for Gender Budget Cells in all ministries; MWCD launched a Gender Budgeting Scheme for capacity building
2008-09Child budgeting through the Statement of Allocation for Welfare of Children (Statement 12)
2022"India @ 75": optimum budgetary resources for women and child welfare across ministries, states and UTs
2024-25Revision of GB format: Part C introduced for schemes where allocation for women is less than 30%
Parts of Gender Budgeting
Part A: women-specific schemes, 100% allocation for women
Part B: pro-women schemes, at least 30% of allocation for women
Part C: schemes with allocation less than 30%

6 · MICRO, SMALL AND MEDIUM ENTERPRISES (MSME)
PYQ 2023 · 10m · manufacturing share and MSME policies (your file)Handout pp.56-61 (teacher's handwriting) and Budget 2026-27 box (p.60)
Understand it firstAn MSME is a business measured by two numbers: how much it has invested and how much it sells in a year. They are the small shops and workshops that supply the big firms, employ most people after agriculture and export a lot. Their daily problem is cash: they get paid late and borrow with difficulty. Memory aid, not from the handout.

Five roles (teacher)
1 Economic growth and contribution to GDP: over 28% of GDP and about 40% of manufacturing output; an engine of growth and equitable development
2 Employment generation: volume (about 111 million people); employment at low capital cost
3 Exports and global competitiveness: more than 40% of exports; diverse sectors (food processing, auto components, pharma); global reach (USA, UAE, China)
4 Promotes innovation and entrepreneurship: base expansion; catalyst role: agile adoption of new tech, rapid market response
5 Fostering inclusive industrial development: geographic and demographic inclusivity (rural and urban); women entrepreneurship (higher subsidy rate, lower certification costs); promotes traditional industry (rural livelihood, artisans; e.g. coir industry)

StageChallenges
1 Registration and classification1.1 Difficulty in classification as proper books are not maintained · 1.2 MSME dwarfism: under-investment to avoid moving up the scale (fear of losing benefits); 98% of MSMEs are micro in nature · 1.3 Non-familiarity and lack of awareness about portals and schemes

6 Logistics6.1 Rural MSMEs: higher logistics costs · 6.2 Lack of cost-effective and efficient supply-chain logistic infrastructure

TReDS: Transforming MSME Financing (handout box)
RBI-regulated digital marketplace; enables timely payments to MSME suppliers by government departments, PSUs and corporates; based on the MSMED Act, 2006.
Key features: post-shipment financing without recourse (based on the buyer's creditworthiness) · auction-based model gives competitive rates from financiers · digital settlement via NPCI for faster, transparent transactions.

7 · MICROFINANCE
PYQ 2021 · 10m · microfinancing women SHGs and the cycle of gender inequality, poverty, malnutritionPYQ 2020 · 15m · micro-finance as an "anti-poverty vaccine": role of SHGsBoth printed on teacher's page 64 · Handout pp.62-64
Understand it firstMicrofinance is tiny loans without collateral to poor households. It reaches women and villages that banks skip. The risk the teacher highlights: when funders chase growth, lending becomes aggressive, households get over-indebted and "impact" is reported with easy numbers rather than real welfare. Memory aid, not from the handout.
  • Definition: RBI defined microfinance as collateral-free loans given to households having annual incomes up to ₹3 lakh.
  • Four purposes (teacher's arrows): last-mile credit · women empowerment · rural financial deepening · livelihood resilience. It leads to asset creation and helps absorb volatility.
  • Importance: channel for advancing grassroots development; the sector has 95% women borrowers and 80% rural clientele; supports credit access for historically underserved households.
  • Reversal in growth in FY25: fall in outstanding loans by 14% (YoY).
Key highlights (infographic)
NBFC-MFIs and banks dominatetogether over 70% of the market; NBFC-MFIs primary leaders, banks second-largest
Significant secondary supportSFBs and NBFCs 28% combined (SFBs 16%, NBFCs 12%)
Geographic focus62% concentrated in East and South
Challenges associated
  • General: difficulty in assessing incomes (reliance on in-house estimation methods) · do not offer tailored credit · incentive structure in MFIs: aggressive lending.
  • Financialisation of MFIs: integration into capital markets (growth-oriented commercial investment); entry of private equity and venture capital investors; focus on portfolio expansion, yield metrics and valuation outcomes (teacher's boxed words: financialisation, growth-driven expansion).
  • Social outcomes ignored: no long-term household welfare.
  • Sectoral stress: overlending · rise in MPA (non-performing assets) · borrower over-indebtedness.
  • Impact washing: use of scale-based "impact indicators" that are easier to report but weakly connected to household welfare. Indicators used: number of borrowers reached · size of loan portfolio · share of women borrowers · geographical spread.
Measures taken: RBI circular (proactive measures)
  • Credit over-exposure + rise in pent-up demand post pandemic → sectoral stress → RBI circular (teacher's red box).
  • Reducing minimum qualifying assets for microfinance from 75% to 60% of total assets for NBFC-MFIs.
  • Stringent guardrails by Self-Regulatory Organisations (SROs) → reduced loan limits and caps on overall borrower indebtedness.
Way forward: restoring the balance
  • Replace "impact-washing" metrics with indicators that track household-level welfare and financial resilience.
  • Alignment of investment incentives: greater emphasis on household balance sheet outcomes.
  • Improve borrower suitability assessments.
  • Strengthen enabling infrastructure, e.g. tools to assess creditworthiness.
  • Responsible lending practices; strengthening institutional resilience; data-driven mechanisms to detect emerging over-indebtedness.

8 · INSOLVENCY AND BANKRUPTCY CODE (IBC)
Handout pp.64-67 (teacher's handwriting + typed IBC Amendment Act 2026)
Understand it firstIBC is a time-bound exit and rescue law: if a company cannot pay, creditors (not the old owners) decide whether to rescue or sell it, within fixed time limits. It replaced many old laws with one Code. The weak spot is delay: cases drag on in the NCLT. The 2026 Amendment adds a faster creditor-led route, group and cross-border insolvency. Memory aid, not from the handout.
  • Mechanism to rehabilitate financial standing or facilitate an honourable exit; unified framework for resolving corporate distress in India.
  • It replaced multiple statutes with a unified Code and created a creditor-driven resolution process within defined timelines.
  • Benefits (teacher's triangle): credit discipline · reduced NPAs · greater predictability.
Key achievements (teacher)
#Achievement
IRecovery rate 31% (improved).
IISuccessful resolutions yielded ₹3.6 lakh crore: 161.1% of liquidation value and 86.1% of fair value (haircut 14%).
IIIResolution of large accounts: 10 of 12 resolved. Resolution timeline decreased from 6-8 years to 2 years.
IVGlobal ratings upgraded from Group C → Group B.
VChange in debtors' behaviour: 28,818 applications for initiation of CIRP withdrawn before admission.
VIForex hedging by firms.
VIIExports: better access to credit for exporting firms.
VIIIBond credit spread: lowering of credit spreads.
IXCreditors recovered 94% of fair value of resolved businesses and 170% of what they would have received through liquidation.
Teacher's definition box
Fair valueestimated value of the company if it is sold as a functioning business under normal market conditions
Liquidation valueestimated value of the company if it is shut down and its assets are sold separately
Check thisp.64 (point II: 161.1% / 86.1% / haircut 14%) and p.65 (point IX: 94% / 170%) give different recovery figures for the same idea (probably different data dates). Both are in the teacher's handwriting. Teacher pages 64 and 65; ask your teacher which to quote.
Issues (teacher, p.65)
#Issue
IDelays: CIRP to be completed within 330 days (mandated) but actual: 713 days overall and 853 days for cases closed in FY25.
IIIssues with NCLT: 98% adjudication rate · 2,593 cases awaiting admission · 4,723 cases pending.
IIIDefaulting debtors retain control until admission → value shifting, fund diversion, asset transfers.
IVDelays in admission of applications: courts verify existence of debt and default; objections from promoters; issues in validating documents.
VSubstantial legal costs for MSMEs.
Solutions (teacher)
  • Enhance the role of ILs (information utilities) in debt verification.
  • Improve the efficiency of tribunals.
  • Expand NCLT's capacity.
  • ADR (alternative dispute resolution) for operational creditors.
  • Enable non-adversarial resolution process of IBC in NCLT in practice.
  • Prepackaged insolvency for MSMEs.

Teacher's page 65 (original): forex hedging to bond spreads, fair value vs liquidation value, issues and solutions of IBC
Check thisp.65: "ILs" is read as Information Utilities (an IBC institution, not named in full on the page) and "4723 cases pending" / "2593 awaiting admission" are read from handwriting; confirm on teacher page 65.
IBC Amendment Act, 2026 (typed pp.66-67)
  • Aim: make the insolvency framework faster, more creditor-responsive and aligned with group insolvency and cross-border insolvency.
Need for the amendment
Six needs
Delays in resolution (litigation, admission-stage disputes, limited tribunal capacity) eroding asset value
Admission-stage uncertainty: admission could be delayed by procedural objections even after default was established
Need for quicker creditor-led resolution: framework was tribunal-heavy; need a faster consensus-based, out-of-court route
No group insolvency framework: stressed firms in groups with common assets, guarantees and interlinked liabilities
Cross-border gaps: foreign creditors, foreign assets, overseas proceedings
Ease of doing business: predictable insolvency system improves credit culture, reduces banking stress, encourages investment
Key provisionDetail
Creditor-Initiated Insolvency Resolution Process (CIIRP)New creditor-initiated route, started by eligible financial creditors; a resolution professional is appointed and a public announcement starts the process; to be completed within 150 days, extendable once by 45 days.
Replacement of Fast-Track InsolvencyCIIRP is the new faster mechanism.
Stronger role of Committee of Creditors in liquidationCoC shall supervise the liquidation process conducted by the liquidator.
Government / statutory duesGovernment dues do not get higher priority merely because a security interest is created by law; Central and State dues are distributed as per the waterfall under Section 53.
Group insolvency frameworkRules for cases involving two or more corporate debtors of the same group.
Cross-border insolvency frameworkCentre may prescribe rules for cross-border proceedings for notified classes of debtors.
Electronic portalTo facilitate insolvency and bankruptcy procedures.
Penalties for misusePenalties for frivolous or vexatious proceedings: ₹1 lakh to ₹2 crore in certain cases.
Challenges
  • Even strong timelines may fail without enough NCLT benches, members, digital infrastructure and technical support.
  • IBC remains largely creditor-driven: protection of operational creditors, workers and MSMEs remains a concern.
  • Cross-border insolvency needs cooperation between Indian tribunals and foreign courts: reciprocity and recognition needed.
  • If debtor-in-possession or out-of-court processes are not monitored, promoters may delay creditor action or retain control without genuine resolution.
Way forward
  • More NCLT benches, technical members, better case management and digital tracking of timelines.
  • Impose costs for unnecessary delays, restrict repeated adjournments, strengthen mediation / settlement windows.
  • Deeper markets for distressed assets through ARCs, special situation funds, transparent auctions, better price discovery.
  • Resolution plans should be fair to operational creditors, workers and small suppliers while preserving creditor-led primacy.
NoteConclusion (handout): the IBC Amendment Act, 2026 is a step towards IBC 2.0: faster resolution, lower procedural delays, stronger creditor confidence and better handling of complex cases. Success depends on institutional capacity, reduced litigation, predictable implementation and protection of all stakeholders. A strong IBC supports banking stability, credit discipline and ease of doing business.
Short forms in section 8

ADR = Alternative Dispute Resolution (mediation or arbitration instead of court)

CIIRP = Creditor-Initiated Insolvency Resolution Process (new faster creditor-started route in the 2026 IBC amendment)

CIRP = Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (the IBC process to rescue a company, with a 330-day limit)

FY25 = Financial Year 2024-25 (April 2024 to March 2025)

IBC = Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (time-bound law to rescue or exit insolvent firms, creditor-led)

MSMEs = Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (plural of MSME)

NCLT = National Company Law Tribunal (tribunal that hears company insolvency cases)

9 · CORPORATE BOND MARKET IN INDIA
Handout pp.68-69 (typed)
Understand it firstA corporate bond is a loan taken by a company directly from many investors instead of from one bank. A deep bond market gives firms long-term money and takes pressure off banks. India's is still small and clubbed at the top: investors only want "AAA" papers. Memory aid, not from the handout.
  • Overview: outstanding corporate bonds grew from ₹17.5 trillion (FY2015) to ₹53.6 trillion (FY2025); yet at about 15-16% of GDP the market is modest, concentrated among top-rated issuers, with private placements dominating public issues.
Benefits of a developed corporate bond market
Four benefits
Diversified funding beyond banks: lowers systemic risk, frees bank capital for priority sectors and MSMEs
Channelling institutional and household savings: long-term instruments for pension funds and insurers; retail gets better returns than deposits (e.g. BHARAT Bond ETFs)
Lowering borrowing costs: bond markets transmit monetary policy faster than bank lending
Efficient pricing and risk management: complements the G-Sec yield curve; enables credit-risk assessment and derivatives such as CDS
Challenges
  • Shallow market: only 15-16% of GDP, illiquid, high cost of capital and over-reliance on banks.
  • Regulatory overlaps: SEBI, RBI and MCA create overlapping compliance burdens and delays.
  • The "AAA" safety trap: institutional investors are over-risk-averse and buy only the safest AAA bonds.
  • Low secondary-market trading: "buy-and-hold"; annual secondary turnover ratio of 0.3; fragmented data and high transaction costs.
  • Tax implications: lack of Section 80C benefits, varied capital gains structures, complex TDS norms.
MNEMONICSALT + RShallow market · AAA trap · Low secondary trading · Tax implications · Regulatory overlaps. Say it: "Corporate bonds need a pinch of SALT, and Reform." (own memory aid; handout order differs)
Cross-country comparison (handout)Detail
Size relative to GDPIndia 14% of GDP (handout text elsewhere says 15-16%) versus China 38%, Malaysia 54%, South Korea 79%
Best practice: EU / Italy"Minibond" market lets unlisted SMEs issue bonds with state credit guarantees
Best practice: MalaysiaDanajamin provides credit guarantees for bonds, helped infrastructure financing without overburdening banks
Check thisp.68 gives the market size as 15-16% of GDP in the overview and 14% of GDP in the cross-country line. Both are in the handout (different years or sources); quote 15-16% with "about". Teacher page: typed p.68.
Reforms and policies undertaken
AuthorityMeasure
SEBIRequest for Quote (RFQ) platform: moves OTC trades to electronic trading · Retail inclusion: minimum face value reduced ₹10 lakh → ₹10,000; Online Bond Platform Providers (OBPPs) formalised
RBIPartial Credit Enhancement (PCE): banks may support lower-rated corporate bonds · Mandatory market borrowing framework: Large Corporates to raise 25% of incremental borrowing through bonds
Ministry of FinanceCDMDF: ₹3,000 crore backstop facility for emergency liquidity, with a government Guarantee Scheme (GSCD) · Budget 2026-27: market-making framework with access to funding and derivatives on corporate bond indices, and total return swaps on corporate bonds
NITI Aayog: three-phase roadmapActions
Phase I: strengthen the foundation (1-2 years)Unified guidelines across SEBI, RBI, MCA · banks and NBFCs as market makers · stronger Credit Rating Agency regulation · real-time bond data system like TRACE · retail participation via low-ticket platforms and Corporate Bond Savings Account
Phase II: expansion and innovation (2-4 years)Unified Corporate Bond Market Development Task Force · structured Corporate Bond Dealer framework · SME bond exchanges with AI-based credit scoring
Phase III: integration, maturity, global alignment (4-6 years)Dedicated Corporate Bond Market Regulator · Corporate Bond Stabilisation Fund · align green and ESG bonds with global standards · link platforms with depositories like Euroclear · use blockchain / DLT for issuance and settlement
NoteConclusion (handout): despite low liquidity, a narrow investor base and regulatory fragmentation, focused reforms can turn the corporate bond market into a deeper source of long-term finance.
10 · PERSISTENTLY HIGH COST OF CAPITAL
Handout p.70 (teacher's handwriting)
Understand it firstThe cost of capital is the price India pays to borrow. The teacher argues it is high not just because banks are inefficient, but because India depends on foreign money to fill a savings gap, so lenders add a risk premium. Growth led by exports and productivity (not by consumption on credit) lowers that premium. Memory aid, not from the handout.
  • 1995-2025: India's weighted-average long-term interest rate was 7.61%.
1 Financial-sector friction
Limited investor depth
Restrictions on capital flows
Shallow corporate bond market
Sovereign risk premia
  • 2 Structural explanation: links the cost of capital to the economy's saving position and external balance. In open-economy macroeconomics, investment must be financed by domestic savings or foreign savings.
  • Persistent CAD: dependence on external capital inflows → a risk premium is priced into interest rates and equity returns. Low CAD → cheaper capital.
Teacher's identity boxReading
C + I + G + X − M = C + S + Tnational-income identity: spending side equals income side
(S − I) = (G − T) + (X − M)with the term marked "Assumed 0" by the teacher
Balanced budget: G = T → S − I = NXsaving minus investment equals net exports
Global lessons
  • Late-industrialising economies lowered capital costs after: productivity-led growth, external surplus generation and sustained export expansion (teacher's triangle).
  • Exports support demand without high inflation.
  • Lower external risk reduces the risk premium in capital costs.
Path (handout flow diagrams)Chain of effects
RISKY PATH: consumption-heavy, credit-led growthDomestic credit expands → consumption demand rises → imports rise faster than exports → CAD pressure increases → dependence on foreign capital increases → currency remains under pressure → risk premium stays high → cost of capital remains high
RIGHT PATH: productivity / export-led growthProductivity rises → export competitiveness increases → foreign exchange earnings rise → CAD pressure reduces / external balance improves → currency credibility improves → risk premium falls → cost of capital falls → private investment increases

11 · PRODUCTION LINKED INCENTIVE (PLI) SCHEME
PYQ 2025 · 15m · rationale, achievements and improvement of PLI (your file)Handout pp.71-74 (typed)
Understand it firstPLI is a pay-for-sales bonus: if a factory in India makes more than last year and meets investment targets, the government pays it a small percentage of the extra sales. It rewards making things here, not just assembling imported parts. Memory aid, not from the handout.
  • Launched: March 2020 in 14 sunrise and labour-intensive sectors.
  • Mechanism: firms get 4-8% cash-back on incremental sales once they meet minimum investment, localisation and production thresholds.
  • Budget envelope: ₹1.97 lakh crore over 5 years.
  • Core aims: (i) shift from import dependence to export-oriented manufacturing; (ii) embed domestic firms in global value chains; (iii) create formal jobs and spur R&D.
Performance
  • FY21-FY25: average annual growth rate (AAGR) of exports from these sectors 10.6%; imports 12.6%.
  • Domestic manufacturing is maturing and leveraging imported intermediate goods for higher-value exports; steady domestic activity with continued reliance on imported inputs and technology.
  • Electronics and mobiles: India flipped from net importer to net exporter of phones; second-largest mobile phone producer.
  • Pharmaceuticals and bulk drugs: domestic API output up; sector value addition 83%.
  • Food processing: ₹3.8 lakh crore sales; strong millet and marine exports.
  • Drones: seven-fold rise in turnover, MSME-led.
PLI sectorExport AAGR (FY21-FY25)Import AAGR (FY21-FY25)
IT hardware77.2%11.0%
ACC batteries45.0%24.9%
Electronics38.8%17.6%
Solar PV23.9%155.4%
Speciality steel22.5%17.5%
BeneficiaryBenefit
Central and state governmentsFaster industrial growth, positive signalling to global investors, boost to manufacturing output by ₹37 lakh crore
Large firms / MNCsPredictable subsidy reduces India-entry risk, scale plants (Foxconn, Samsung, Dixon)
MSMEs and start-ups70+ direct beneficiaries, cluster spill-overs in drones and textiles; creating "champions" for GVCs; forward and backward linkages
Workers / skill ecosystem12 lakh new jobs; catalyses vocational education demand
Consumers and exportersCheaper domestically made phones and LEDs; diversified export basket
EnvironmentSolar-module and EV-battery PLIs support decarbonisation
Key structural challenges
  • Reliance on imported inputs and technology.
  • Assembly-heavy value addition: Economic Survey 2024-25 flags "limited progress in design and component manufacturing" (local value-add in smartphones still about 18%).
  • Slow incentive uptake: less than 12% of the ₹1.97 lakh crore kitty paid out so far.
  • Uneven sectoral traction: electronics and pharma corner 70% of subsidies; steel, textiles and ACC batteries lag.
  • WTO compliance: output-linked cash subsidies could face action if shown to be contingent on exports.
  • Logistics and supply-chain gaps: high freight and electricity costs.
  • May go against domestic companies: deep-pocketed foreign firms may gain more.
Policy recalibration underway
  • Sunset clause: existing PLIs to wind down by mid-2026; the Centre is pivoting to a ₹22,919 crore Component Manufacturing PLI.
  • New candidate sectors: NITI Aayog proposes extending PLI to labour-intensive leather, footwear and furniture.
Way forward
  • "Component first" push: capex-linked incentives for PCBs, displays, EV power electronics, textile machinery to lift domestic value-addition above 40%.
  • Tighter milestone-based payouts after audited localisation and R&D.
  • Green conditionalities: link part of incentives to energy-efficiency and circular-economy metrics.
  • Cluster infrastructure and skill hubs: integrate PLI zones with PM Gati-Shakti corridors; skilling via NSDC.
  • MSME onboarding: smaller slabs with lower turnover thresholds plus a Quality-Upgradation Fund (NITI).
  • Sunrise-sector rotation: use impact evaluations (IIM-Ahmedabad, NITI) to retire under-performing segments and redirect funds to semiconductors, green-hydrogen equipment and biotech.

TRAPS AND EXAM-HALL RULES
TrapWhy it fools youExam-hall rule
GST 2.0 has "no compensation scheme".The handout says no compensation scheme; instead assurance of timely transfers, versus 14% growth compensation for 5 years in GST 1.0.Write both halves of the sentence.
Debt-GDP replaces the fiscal deficit.Debt-GDP becomes the anchor; the fiscal deficit stays the operational tool.Say "anchor" and "operational tool".
16th FC cut the states' share.States' share remains 41%; the formula and grants change.Name what changed: GDP-contribution added, tax-effort removed.
MSME figures from different pages.GDP 28% / 30.1% / 31.1% are different sources and years.Quote one figure with its source (Survey 2025-26: 31.1%).
MSME limits: investment versus turnover.Micro: investment ₹2.5 crore, turnover ₹10 crore (revised), not the other way round.Write both with "investment" and "turnover".
IBC: 330 days versus actual.330 days is the mandated CIRP limit; actual is 713 / 853 days.Write "mandated" and "actual".
IBC recovery figures.Two sets appear in the teacher's notes (161.1% / 86.1% and 94% / 170%).Quote with "as per the handout" and one set only.
PLI incentive base.PLI pays on incremental sales, not total sales; 4-8%.Always say "incremental".

SELF-TEST (answer key below)
  • Q1. GST 2.0 de-merit rate: (a) 28% (b) 40% (c) 12% (d) 35%
  • Q2. States' share in central taxes under the 16th FC: (a) 42% (b) 41% (c) 40% (d) 45%
  • Q3. Gender Budget Part B means: (a) 100% women-specific (b) at least 30% for women (c) below 30% (d) none
  • Q4. Revised turnover limit for a small enterprise: (a) ₹50 crore (b) ₹100 crore (c) ₹250 crore (d) ₹25 crore
  • Q5. TReDS is based on which Act? (a) IBC 2016 (b) MSMED Act 2006 (c) FRBM 2003 (d) Companies Act
  • Q6. CIRP mandated time limit is: (a) 150 days (b) 270 days (c) 330 days (d) 713 days
  • Q7. PLI mechanism pays: (a) 4-8% of incremental sales (b) 25% of stipend (c) 10% of capex (d) 1% of turnover
  • Q8. Under the CIIRP the process is to be completed within: (a) 90 days (b) 150 days extendable by 45 (c) 330 days (d) 180 days
NoteAnswer key: Q1 b (Merit 5%, standard 18%, de-merit 40%.) · Q2 b (Retained at 41%.) · Q3 b (Part A 100%, Part C below 30%.) · Q4 b (Micro 10, Small 100, Medium 500.) · Q5 b (RBI-regulated; MSMED Act, 2006.) · Q6 c (713 is the actual overall.) · Q7 a (On meeting investment and localisation thresholds.) · Q8 b (IBC Amendment Act 2026.)

ABBREVIATION COLUMN
Abbreviation columnEvery short form in this chapter, with its full form and a one-line plain meaning. The meanings are plain-language aids to help revision: verify them before quoting in an answer.

AAA: Highest credit rating. safest rating for a bond

AAGR: Average Annual Growth Rate. average yearly growth over a period

ACC: Advanced Chemistry Cell. battery technology covered by a PLI scheme

ADR: Alternative Dispute Resolution. mediation or arbitration instead of court

AI: Artificial Intelligence. computer systems that do tasks needing human-like learning or judgement

AIF: Alternative Investment Fund. pooled private investment vehicle (Category II)

API: Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient. the bulk drug that makes a medicine work

ASBA: Application Supported by Blocked Amount. IPO payment method where money stays in your account until allotment

ASUSE: Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises. survey of small unorganised enterprises, now quarterly

BHARAT: Bharat Bond (ETF). exchange-traded fund of government-company bonds

CAD: Current Account Deficit. imports of goods, services and income exceed exports

CAGR: Compound Annual Growth Rate. smoothed yearly growth rate

CDMDF: Corporate Debt Market Development Fund. ₹3,000 crore backstop for market stress

CDS: Credit Default Swap. insurance-like contract against a bond default

CGTMSE: Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises. gives guarantee cover on collateral-free MSE loans

CIIRP: Creditor-Initiated Insolvency Resolution Process. new faster creditor-started route in the 2026 IBC amendment

CIRP: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process. the IBC process to rescue a company, with a 330-day limit

COVID: Coronavirus Disease 2019. the pandemic that hit GST collections and compensation

CPSE: Central Public Sector Enterprise. a company owned by the central government

DISCOM: Distribution Company. state power distribution utility

DISHA: Disha programme for women in science. scheme named in the Gender Budget infographic (full form: verify in source)

DLT: Distributed Ledger Technology. blockchain-type shared record

ESG: Environmental, Social and Governance. sustainability criteria for bonds

EU: European Union. the bloc of European countries

EV: Electric Vehicle. battery-run vehicle

FC: Finance Commission. constitutional body that recommends how taxes are shared between Centre and states

FCI: Food Corporation of India. agency that buys and stores foodgrains; its borrowings can be off-budget

FD: Fiscal Deficit. total spending minus total receipts excluding borrowing; the amount the government must borrow

FHI: Fiscal Health Index. NITI Aayog index scoring states' finances

FRBM: Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act, 2003. law setting deficit and debt limits

FSA: Financial Sector Assessment (World Bank). report that found 27% of MSMEs name finance as top obstacle

FY: Financial Year. April to March accounting year (FY25 = 2024-25)

FY2015: Financial Year 2014-15. base year for the corporate bond figure

FY2025: Financial Year 2024-25. latest year for the corporate bond figure

FY21: Financial Year 2020-21.

FY23: Financial Year 2022-23. April 2022 to March 2023

FY25: Financial Year 2024-25. April 2024 to March 2025

FY31: Financial Year 2030-31. the year by which the debt target is to be reached

GB: Gender Budget. allocations for women within the Budget

GBS: Gender Budget Statement. annual statement of allocations for women

GDP: Gross Domestic Product. value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a year

GSCD: Guarantee Scheme for Corporate Debt. government guarantee backing the CDMDF

GSDP: Gross State Domestic Product. the size of a state's economy

GST: Goods and Services Tax. India's indirect tax on goods and services

HFI: High-Frequency Indicator. one such indicator

IBC: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. time-bound law to rescue or exit insolvent firms, creditor-led

IMF: International Monetary Fund. global body whose statistical standards PPI follows

IPO: Initial Public Offering. first sale of shares to the public

IT: Information Technology. software and computer-based services

ITC: Input Tax Credit. GST paid on inputs that can be set off against GST on sales

KISAN: PM-KISAN. income support to farmers, listed under Part C

MCA: Ministry of Corporate Affairs. the ministry revising the PM Internship Scheme

MDAVF: Maharashtra Defence and Aerospace Venture Fund. ₹330 crore state fund for MSMEs

MPA: (as written by teacher) likely NPA. non-performing asset; check teacher page 63

MSME: Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises. small firms by investment and turnover limits

MSMED: Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development (Act, 2006). law that governs MSME definitions and delayed-payment rules

MSMEs: Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises. plural of MSME

MWCD: Ministry of Women and Child Development. nodal ministry for gender budgeting

NBFC: Non-Banking Financial Company. lender that is not a bank

NCLT: National Company Law Tribunal. tribunal that hears company insolvency cases

NITI: National Institution for Transforming India. government think tank (NITI Aayog)

NPA: Non-Performing Asset. a bank loan that has stopped being repaid

NPCI: National Payments Corporation of India. operator of retail payment systems

NRLM: National Rural Livelihoods Mission. mission that promotes SHGs

NSDC: National Skill Development Corporation. skilling agency

NSSF: National Small Savings Fund. pool of small-savings money lent to the government

NX: Net Exports. exports minus imports

ODOP: One District One Product. scheme to promote one product per district

ODR: Online Dispute Resolution. digital settlement of disputes

ONDC: Open Network for Digital Commerce. open e-commerce network that lowers commissions

OTC: Over-The-Counter. trades done directly between parties, not on an exchange

PCE: Partial Credit Enhancement. bank support that lifts a bond's rating

PLI: Production Linked Incentive. incentive paid on extra sales of goods made in India

PM: Prime Minister. head of the Union government

PMI: Purchasing Managers' Index. survey index of business activity; used as a growth proxy

PSB: Public Sector Bank. government-owned bank

PSE: Public Sector Enterprise. a government-owned company

PV: Photovoltaic. solar cell technology

RAMP: Raising and Accelerating MSME Performance. World Bank-assisted MSME programme

RBI: Reserve Bank of India. India's central bank

RFQ: Request for Quote. electronic platform for bond trades

RODTEP: Remission of Duties and Taxes on Exported Products. refunds embedded taxes on exports

SEBI: Securities and Exchange Board of India. stock and bond market regulator

SHG: Self-Help Group. small group of women that saves and borrows together

SHRI: PM Schools for Rising India (PM SHRI). central school-upgrading scheme listed under Part B

SME: Small and Medium Enterprise. small and mid-sized firm

SMEs: Small and Medium Enterprises. plural of SME

SRI: Self-Reliant India (Fund). equity fund for MSMEs

SRO: Self-Regulatory Organisation. industry body that sets conduct rules for members

TDS: Tax Deducted at Source. tax the payer deducts and deposits before paying income

TEAM: Trade Enablement and Marketing initiative. onboards MSMEs onto ONDC

TRACE: Trade Reporting and Compliance Engine (US). real-time bond trade data system used as a model

TReDS: Trade Receivables Discounting System. platform where MSME invoices are sold to financiers for early cash

UAE: United Arab Emirates. one of MSMEs' export markets

UAP: Udyam Assist Platform. route to register informal micro enterprises

UHT: Ultra-High Temperature (milk). long-life packaged milk; made zero GST

UPI: Unified Payments Interface. instant mobile payment system

USA: United States of America. one of the countries the handout names for school-level vocational exposure

WTO: World Trade Organization. global trade-rules body

ZED: Zero Effect, Zero Defect. quality and environment certification for MSMEs
